Geopolitics and oil

US President Donald Trump told Newsmax that he would not use nuclear weapons against Iran and did not expect US ground troops to be sent into the country. He said, however, that the US may have to strike Pickaxe Mountain, an underground site near Natanz linked to Iran’s nuclear programme. The comments largely restated earlier positions, and Trump said last week that the US would not attack Iran before next month’s midterm elections.

Separately, there were unconfirmed reports of possible launches of anti-ship ballistic missiles, anti-ship cruise missiles and drones towards port anchorages at Sharjah, Ras Al Khaimah or Jebel Ali in the United Arab Emirates, or nearby areas of the Strait of Hormuz. The reports had not been verified at the time of writing.

Oil prices edged only slightly lower over the session.

FX and gold

Gold traded around $25 higher. Several large Indian mutual funds, including Kotak, UTI and HDFC, halted bulk gold ETF subscriptions ahead of the festive season, reportedly after a nudge from SEBI, removing a seasonal support for gold as India seeks to shield the rupee.

The US dollar eased slightly ahead of remarks from Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh.

Central banks

Warsh declined to signal the Fed’s next move, saying he does not believe in saying what he might do at meetings for the rest of 2026. Speaking at an IMF session in Bangkok, he said the world has broadly conformed to the Fed’s expectations since its September rate hike. He described the October and December meetings as the crystallising moments for judging output, employment and inflation. He also said AI is likely to boost demand before it delivers supply-side gains.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack warned that if an inflationary mindset takes hold among households and businesses, the Fed may need to act more aggressively. She said businesses are facing significant input cost pressures and that financial conditions do not currently appear restrictive.

Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said second-round effects from high energy prices have been subdued so far, but that it is too early to form a firm view. He described above-target UK inflation as enormously frustrating and said Middle East news is the biggest factor moving UK government bond yields. Markets have been pricing a high chance of a Bank of England rate rise on 5 November.

Companies

Moody’s changed its outlook on Nike to negative and affirmed its A2 rating, citing a turnaround taking longer than it had expected. The agency expects Nike’s revenue and earnings to decline through the fiscal year ending May 2027 and into fiscal 2028.

Tesla unveiled its long-delayed next-generation Roadster, which uses thrusters developed with SpaceX to flip and land in mid-air. Reservations require $50,000 upfront, the price has not been confirmed, and production is due to start in 2028, years after deliveries were first promised for 2020.

Asia data

Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports rose about 68% in September from a year earlier, well above the roughly 32% expected in a Reuters poll and a sixth straight month of growth above 20%. The gain was driven mainly by non-electronics, chiefly ship and boat structures, though electronics exports also surged.

item.title: Warsh won’t prejudge rest of 2026, names October and December as decision points
item.description:
With no guidance from the chair, short-dated Treasuries and the dollar will take their lead from data before the 27–28 October meeting, which points to bigger reactions to releases. His comment that events have broadly matched expectations leans slightly hawkish, since the September projections pointed to another hike this year. Oil remains a key input: fuel-driven inflation tied to the Iran war is the main source of upside price pressure, so moves in crude will feed directly into hike pricing. A hawkish-leaning Fed has tended to weigh on gold rather than support it.

---

Earlier, Hammack no so reticent on forward guidance:

  • Fed's Hammack questions whether Fed policy is tight enough as inflation risks build

---

Warsh came to Bangkok and said, in effect, watch the data, not me, which is exactly what he has been promising to do.

Summary:

  • Warsh said he does not believe in saying what he might do at meetings for the rest of 2026
  • He said the October and December meetings will be the crystallising moments for judging output, jobs and inflation
  • Since the September meeting, the world has broadly conformed to Fed expectations, he said
  • He called a structural investment surge the biggest upside in the global economy, crediting good policies
  • AI will hit demand before supply, will make the economy more productive over time, and has an uncertain near-term impact on jobs, he said
  • The Fed will hold a field hearing on AI in the San Francisco Bay Area on 16 November

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal the central bank’s next move on Friday. He said he does not believe in saying what he might do at meetings for the rest of 2026, and pointed to the Fed’s October and December meetings as the moments when policymakers will take stock.

Speaking at an IMF session in Bangkok, held during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, Warsh said the world has broadly conformed to the Fed’s expectations since its September policy meeting. He said the Fed has made clear it will deliver price stability, but that he does not believe in prejudging meetings. Policymakers will make their judgements at the October and December meetings, which he described as the crystallising moments for assessing output, employment and inflation.

The refusal to give guidance was no surprise. Warsh has repeatedly argued that the Fed should say less about its intentions so that markets form their own view of the economy, and he has said he opposes signalling decisions in advance. Friday’s comments put that approach [into practice](LINK TO QUIETER FED PIECE), leaving investors to rely on incoming data ahead of the 27 and 28 October meeting.

His remark that events have broadly matched expectations is still worth noting. In September the Fed raised rates by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4.00%, its first hike since 2023, and most officials projected at least one further increase this year. If the outlook has unfolded as expected, that suggests he sees little reason so far to depart from that path, although he stopped short of saying so.

Warsh devoted much of his remarks to investment and artificial intelligence. He described a structural investment surge, which he attributed to good policies, as the most important upside development in the global economy. On AI, he said the technology would make the economy more productive and create more wealth, but that the path would be bumpy, and that its near-term impact on employment is uncertain. He said AI is likely to boost demand before it delivers the supply-side gains that could ease inflation, and that it should also help central banks gain confidence in their data.

That sequencing matters for policy. If AI-related investment lifts spending now while productivity gains arrive later, it adds to near-term inflation pressure. That is consistent with Warsh’s earlier argument that current rates are not restricting activity.

Warsh also said the Fed’s policies spill over to the rest of the world, but that other countries’ policies spill back to the US too. He added that the Fed will hold a field hearing on AI in the San Francisco Bay Area on 16 November, as part of its task force work.

The next markers are US data ahead of the 27 and 28 October meeting, and whether other Fed officials fill the gap left by the chair’s silence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tesla unveils thruster-powered Roadster with $50,000 deposit, production slated for 2028
item.description:
The Roadster is unlikely to move Tesla’s fundamentals. Estimated volumes of around 2,000 a year are tiny next to the company’s total sales, so any share reaction is likely to be about sentiment and brand rather than earnings. Investor focus remains on Tesla’s AI, robotaxi and robotics ambitions, which carry far more weight in its valuation. The $50,000 upfront deposits bring in some early cash, but the bigger takeaway for investors may be the delay record, which keeps execution risk front of mind.

---

Yesterday:

  • Barclays sees possible Tesla-SpaceX merger announcement before December

---

Tesla’s new Roadster can flip itself in mid-air, which is more than can be said for its delivery schedule, now pointing at 2028.

Summary:

  • Tesla unveiled its next-generation Roadster at a SpaceX test site in Texas on Thursday
  • Its SpaceX-developed thrusters let it flip and land; Musk claims 0–60 mph in under a second and a top speed above 230 mph
  • Reservations need $5,000 down plus $45,000 within 10 days, and a premium version needs a $250,000 deposit
  • The price is unconfirmed but expected to top $250,000
  • Production is due in 2028, after deliveries were first promised for 2020
  • One analyst estimates around 2,000 sales a year, against the 1.6 million vehicles Tesla sold last year

Tesla finally showed off its long-delayed new Roadster on Thursday, complete with SpaceX-developed thrusters that let the car flip itself in mid-air. Buyers will need deep pockets and plenty of patience, though, with production not due to start until 2028.

At a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, the two-seater drove upside down on a ramp, then used its built-in thrusters to turn and land. Chief Executive Elon Musk said the car can reach 60 mph from a standstill in under a second and hit a top speed above 230 mph, and suggested the production version could aim even higher. The thruster system uses 10 nozzles and 250 kilograms of compressed air, and Musk said the tanks can recharge while driving. It was not immediately clear whether the stunt features could be used legally on public roads.

Securing a place in the queue is costly. Tesla is asking for a $5,000 deposit followed by a further $45,000 within 10 days, taking the upfront commitment to $50,000. A higher-specification version requires a $250,000 deposit. Tesla has not confirmed a price, although it is expected to exceed $250,000, well above the roughly $200,000 base price quoted when the car was first unveiled.

The timeline remains the biggest question mark. Tesla first showed a next-generation Roadster in 2017 and said deliveries would begin in 2020, before a series of delays. Thursday’s event itself came two weeks after a planned 1 October reveal was postponed by severe weather.

For investors, the Roadster is a brand statement rather than a business driver. Musk himself has played down its financial importance, and one equity analyst estimates sales of around 2,000 cars a year, a small fraction of the 1.6 million vehicles Tesla sold last year. The company’s valuation rests far more on its push into artificial intelligence, self-driving and robotics, including its Cybercab robotaxi and Optimus humanoid robots.

That makes the Roadster a halo product: one designed to show off engineering ambition and keep the brand in the headlines, rather than move the needle on earnings. Its real test will come in 2028, if Tesla can turn a stunt car into a road car on schedule. Given the history, investors may want to see it before they believe it. 

Until 2028?

item.title: Bailey says UK second-round inflation effects subdued so far, too early to judge
item.description:
The comments are more balanced than Bailey’s late-September warnings, and could take a little heat out of heavily priced November hike bets in short-dated gilts and sterling, without ruling a move out. His point that Middle East news is the biggest driver of gilt yields puts oil and gas prices at the centre of the UK rate outlook: renewed escalation in the Iran war would lift energy costs and strengthen the case for a hike, while any easing would weaken it. Next week’s September inflation data and the 28 October Budget are the next catalysts.

---

Background:

  • BOE, Bailey, Bangkok. What could possibly go wrong? Preview and 3 questions for the Governor

---

Bailey is frustrated with inflation but not yet alarmed by it, which leaves November live without giving hike-hungry markets the nod they wanted.

Summary:

  • Bailey said second-round effects from high energy prices have been subdued so far
  • He said it is too early to form strong views, and that businesses are emphasising cost-cutting
  • He called above-target UK inflation enormously frustrating
  • The UK economy is more resilient than expected but not as strong as needed, he said
  • Middle East news is the biggest factor moving gilt yields, he said
  • Bank Rate is 3.75%, after a 6-3 hold in September; the next decision is on 5 November

Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said on Friday that higher energy prices have so far had only a limited knock-on effect on wider British prices, but that it is too early to form a firm view. That leaves the door open to a rate rise without signalling that one is imminent.

Speaking at the Institute of International Finance’s annual meeting in Bangkok, held alongside the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, Bailey said the evidence on so-called second-round effects has been quite subdued. These are effects where higher energy costs feed into wages and the prices of other goods and services. He added that businesses are emphasising cost-cutting, rather than passing costs on.

At the same time, Bailey described above-target UK inflation as enormously frustrating. He said the economy has proved more resilient than the Bank expected, but is not as strong as it needs to be, and that news from the Middle East is the biggest factor driving UK government bond yields.

The comments matter because markets have been betting heavily on a rate rise at the Bank’s next decision on 5 November. Bank Rate stands at 3.75%, and at the September meeting the Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold, with three members preferring an immediate increase. Bailey voted with the majority. In late September, however, he warned that persistently high energy prices would make it harder to keep rates on hold, a shift in tone that helped push hike expectations higher.

Friday’s remarks are more balanced. Describing second-round effects as subdued is consistent with the Bank’s September assessment, and suggests Bailey is not yet convinced the energy shock is becoming embedded in wage and price setting. That is the key test for the MPC majority. His frustration over inflation, however, signals little tolerance for a prolonged overshoot, so the comments stop short of pushing back against a November move.

His point on gilt yields underlines how far UK rates now depend on oil and gas prices tied to the Iran war. A further rise in energy costs would strengthen the case for tightening, while an easing in Middle East tensions would weaken it.

The next markers are UK September inflation data next week, the 28 October Budget, and the Bank’s November decision, which will come with fresh forecasts. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Ethereum whale’s $13.45M loss reflects a year-long exit, not a fresh ETH dump
item.description:
Ethereum whale’s $13.45 million loss is a year-long exit, not a fresh dump

A wallet that began buying Ethereum (ETH) near last year’s market peak has now moved almost its entire position onto exchanges. On-chain analyst Ai Yi flagged the activity, Odaily reported it, and Binance News carried it on Friday. The headline figure, a potential $13.45 million loss on 15,361 ETH, checks out arithmetically. But it describes twelve months of activity, not a single sale this week, and that difference matters for how traders should read it.

What the wallet actually did

The investor started buying in September 2025 at around $4,600 and kept adding as prices fell. In total, 15,810 ETH was withdrawn from exchanges at an average cost of about $4,100, roughly $65 million. Between October 2025 and October 2026, the wallet sent 15,361 ETH back to exchanges at an average price of about $3,226. The most recent deposit came a few hours before the report, but its size was not disclosed. The wallet still holds 572 ETH.

Why a deposit is not the same as a sale

Moving coins onto an exchange often comes before selling, which is why analysts track these transfers. But on-chain data shows that coins moved, not that they were sold. Exchange deposits can also be used as collateral for borrowing or for internal transfers. The $13.45 million figure is therefore an estimate. It assumes every deposited coin was sold at the market price on the day it arrived.

The averaging-down lesson

Buying more as prices fell did bring this investor’s average cost down from about $4,600 to about $4,100. The catch is that it also grew the position while the market kept falling. Ethereum has since dropped well below both levels. ETH was consolidating around $2,500 on October 12, after sliding from roughly $2,725 on October 5 to around $2,474 on October 9.

My read is that the gradual exit limited the damage. Holding the full position until today, at roughly $2,500 per coin, would have meant a paper loss of about $1,600 per ETH, or around $24.6 million. The broader point for readers is that averaging down only helps if the asset eventually recovers. Without a plan for when to stop adding, it can turn a mistimed entry into a much larger one.

Putting one whale in context

This wallet’s selling is small next to the flows moving through Ethereum ETFs. Its full year of deposits, about 15,361 ETH, is less than the roughly 22,440 ETH that left BlackRock’s ETHA in a single day on October 9. kucoin

Those fund flows have been heavy:

  • Investors pulled about $542 million from US spot Ethereum ETFs in the week ending October 9, which was described as the largest weekly outflow since January. cryptobriefingcoinstats
  • Ethereum funds lost a further $85.4 million on October 12. kucoin

A caution on reading those numbers: ETF outflows are net redemptions and do not necessarily mean all of the underlying ETH was sold on the open market. Like the whale’s deposits, they show money leaving, not exactly where the coins ended up.

What could change the interpretation

The story rests on the analyst correctly identifying the wallet. If those addresses turn out to belong to a custodian, fund or exchange-linked entity, the “underwater investor” framing falls away. On the other hand, if several wallets that bought near the 2025 highs show the same pattern, that would point to wider capitulation among late buyers, not one person’s exit. Capitulation here means holders giving up and selling at a loss.

What to watch next

  • The remaining 572 ETH: if they move to an exchange, the wallet’s exit is complete.
  • Other high-cost holders: look for similar deposit patterns among wallets that bought in the $4,000 to $4,800 range.
  • ETF flows and price together: if ETF outflows ease and ETH holds near $2,500, that would suggest selling pressure is fading. If outflows continue and price keeps slipping, late buyers may still be heading for the exits.

The practical takeaway is to treat single-whale headlines as a prompt to check flows and price, not as a signal on their own. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Google’s 40-fold quantum leap: big for Willow, smaller for Alphabet’s share price
item.description:
The result is a research milestone rather than a revenue event, so any lasting effect on Alphabet shares is likely to be limited, given the company’s value rests mainly on search, cloud and AI. Smaller pure-play quantum stocks are more sensitive to sector headlines and could see sharper sentiment-driven moves. The encryption angle may resurface in crypto markets, but the gap between this result and what code-breaking would require is wide. The bigger signal is competitive: it strengthens Google’s standing in the race for error-corrected quantum computing.

-

Google has made quantum computing’s most expensive ingredient much cheaper to cook, but it is still working in a test kitchen, not a factory.

Summary:

  • Google says magic state cultivation cut errors about 40-fold on its Willow chip
  • The result, published in Science, produced magic states with 99.99% fidelity
  • Magic states are a key bottleneck, with some estimates putting their production cost at up to 95% of machine capacity
  • The test used at most 54 of Willow’s 105 qubits, and only about 8% of attempts passed every check
  • Google says larger-scale demonstrations are still needed and has given no timeline
  • Breaking RSA-2048 encryption would need magic states about a million times cleaner

Google says it has demonstrated a way around one of the biggest bottlenecks in quantum computing, cutting errors in a crucial resource by about 40-fold on its Willow chip. The result brings practical, error-corrected machines a step closer but stops well short of making them a near-term reality.

The company’s Quantum AI team set out the work in a paper published in the journal Science and a blog post on Thursday. It centres on so-called magic states, a special type of quantum state that quantum computers need to carry out the full range of calculations that would make them useful. Producing high-quality magic states has been extremely costly, with some estimates suggesting it could take up as much as 95% of a machine’s capacity.

Google’s approach, called magic state cultivation, was proposed by its own researchers in 2024 but had until now been tested only in theory and simulation. It works by growing a rough magic state in a small section of the chip and running repeated error checks, discarding any attempt in which a flaw is detected. On Willow, the technique cut errors by roughly 40 times compared with states produced without it, and delivered magic states with a fidelity of 99.99%.

The significance lies in efficiency. If magic states can be made cheaply and reliably, more of a future quantum computer’s capacity can be devoted to actual calculations, reducing the size and cost of machines needed to solve useful problems.

The caveats are substantial. The experiment used at most 54 of Willow’s 105 qubits, and only about 8% of cultivation attempts passed every check. Google itself said the method still needs to be proven at larger scale and that many technical challenges remain, and it gave no timeline for commercially useful machines.

The result also feeds into the debate over quantum risks to encryption, including the cryptography that protects bitcoin and online banking. For now that risk remains distant: breaking widely used RSA-2048 encryption would require magic states roughly a million times cleaner than those Google has produced.

For investors, the announcement is a research milestone rather than a commercial one, and it is unlikely to change the outlook for Alphabet, whose value rests mainly on search, cloud and artificial intelligence. It does reinforce Google’s position in the race to build error-corrected quantum computers. Headlines like this have tended to drive sharp moves in smaller, pure-play quantum stocks.

The next markers will be whether Google can show cultivation working at larger scale, and whether independent researchers confirm the results. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: FX option expiries for 16 October 10am New York cut
item.description:

item.title: Goldman: Warsh’s quieter Fed: why less guidance could mean more market volatility
item.description:
Less forward guidance shifts the burden onto data, which points to bigger moves in short-dated Treasuries, the dollar and rate-sensitive equities around key releases, as this week’s CPI reaction showed. Bond volatility may stay elevated even if the eventual Fed path matches the consensus for a single December hike. Oil is a central variable in that regime: with the Iran war keeping energy costs high, every swing in crude feeds directly into inflation expectations, and with less Fed guidance to anchor them, into rate pricing. Gold is likely to keep trading off yields and hike expectations rather than geopolitical headlines.

---

Warsh wants markets to stop staring at the Fed and start reading the economy, but after 15 years of hand-holding, the first steps without guidance may be wobbly ones.

Summary:

  • Warsh has set up five task forces, including one on communications, and wants the Fed to reveal less of its internal thinking
  • He opposes giving guidance on upcoming rate decisions
  • Goldman’s Investment Strategy Group expects changes to be gradual, but flags concerns about longer policy lags and extra volatility
  • Rate pricing has already swung sharply on data, including a slump in October hike odds in late September and a jump in yields after this week’s CPI
  • Most major banks expect one more Fed hike in December
  • Warsh speaks in Bangkok on Friday, ahead of the 27–28 October FOMC meeting

For more than a decade, investors have been trained to read the Federal Reserve’s every word. Kevin Warsh wants to break the habit, and Goldman Sachs is warning clients that weaning markets off Fed guidance could come with a price: longer policy lags and more volatility.

The Fed chair, who speaks at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok on Friday, has set up five task forces to review how the central bank works. They cover communications, the balance sheet, data sources, productivity and jobs, and the inflation framework. Communications is the one most likely to change how markets trade. Warsh has argued that the Fed should say less about its internal thinking so that investors form their own view of the economy, likening it to watching the game rather than the official. He has also said he opposes giving guidance on whether the Fed will hike, cut or hold at upcoming meetings.

In its latest quarterly update for clients, Goldman’s Investment Strategy Group said any changes from the task forces are likely to be gradual. But it flagged a concern shared by some investors. If the Fed tells markets less, it may take longer for policy to work through financial conditions, and the adjustment could be bumpier for both markets and the real economy.

The logic is straightforward. Forward guidance has long worked as a policy tool in its own right. When the Fed signals its path, bond yields, mortgage rates and the dollar move ahead of any decision, doing part of the tightening or easing in advance. Take the signals away and markets must wait for the data, and for the decisions themselves, to adjust. That could mean bigger moves on key releases and more frequent repricing between meetings.

There are early signs of what that looks like. In the space of a week in late September, futures pricing for an October hike swung from around 70% to below 40% as softer inflation data and comments from a senior Fed official changed the picture. Goldman itself pushed back its expected next hike from October to December at the start of the month. This week’s hotter-than-expected consumer price data then lifted Treasury yields sharply as traders added to bets on further tightening.

The September hike, the first since 2023, came with a statement that offered no explicit guidance on future moves. That leaves markets leaning heavily on data and on individual officials, with regional presidents such as Cleveland’s Beth Hammack filling some of the gap with their own views.

Warsh’s case has merit. Heavy guidance can lock a central bank into a path that the data no longer support, and can encourage markets to bet on the Fed rather than on the economy. A market that does its own homework may also price risk more honestly. The trade-off is that the transition period, while investors relearn how to read the economy without a script, is likely to be noisier.

For traders, that suggests a regime in which economic releases matter more and Fed meetings matter differently. Short-dated Treasuries, the dollar and rate-sensitive equities are likely to be the most exposed. Bond volatility may stay elevated even if the Fed’s path ends up close to what Wall Street expects, with most major banks now forecasting a single further hike in December.

Friday’s appearance in Bangkok is a test case. If Warsh sticks to his script and offers little on October, markets will have to make their own call before the Fed meets on 27 and 28 October, which is exactly the point. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump draws two red lines on Iran but keeps Pickaxe Mountain strike in play
item.description:
The remarks are unlikely to move oil much on their own, since they repeat earlier positions, but they reinforce the geopolitical risk premium in crude by keeping a strike on Iran’s remaining nuclear infrastructure on the table. The real oil risk lies in Hormuz: any escalation that triggers further Iranian attacks on tankers would tighten already constrained flows and push prices back above $100. Ruling out nuclear weapons and ground troops slightly reduces tail risk, while Trump’s pre-midterm pause offers near-term breathing room. As throughout the conflict, higher oil feeds inflation and Fed hike expectations, which has weighed on gold rather than lifting it.

--

Trump has taken nukes and boots off the table, but not the bombers, and for oil traders the mountain near Natanz is still on the map.

Summary:

  • Trump told Newsmax he would not use nuclear weapons on Iran and does not see US troops on the ground there
  • He said the US may have to go after Pickaxe Mountain, an underground site near Natanz linked to Iran’s nuclear programme
  • He said he is talking to Russia and China about denuclearisation, without giving details
  • Last week, Trump said the US would not attack Iran before the November midterms
  • CBS News has reported US plans to use a massive conventional bomb against Iranian military sites if ordered
  • Hormuz disruption and tanker attacks keep US crude near $97, despite accelerated IEA stock releases

US President Donald Trump said he would not use nuclear weapons against Iran and did not expect to send ground troops into the country. He kept open the possibility of a strike on Pickaxe Mountain, the underground site near Natanz that analysts link to Iran’s nuclear programme.

Speaking in an interview with Newsmax, Trump said the US may have to go after Pickaxe Mountain. He also said he was talking to Russia and China about denuclearisation, though he gave no detail on those discussions.

Pickaxe Mountain, known in Iran as Kuh-e Kolang, is a complex of tunnels built into a mountain a few miles from Natanz. Iran declared it a centrifuge assembly site in 2021, and analysts estimate it is buried about 100 metres underground. It is widely described as the last significant nuclear-linked site in Iran to have escaped strikes, and Trump has repeatedly threatened to hit it since July. Analysts have cautioned that even the heaviest US bunker-busting bombs may not guarantee its destruction.

The comments add to mixed signals from Washington. Last week Trump said the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections in early November and pointed to productive conversations with Tehran. At the same time, CBS News has reported that the White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use one of the largest US conventional bombs against military sites in Iran, should the president order it. Ruling out nuclear weapons and ground troops narrows the range of options, but leaves air strikes on the table.

For energy markets, the key question is what any escalation would mean for the Strait of Hormuz, through which a large share of the world’s oil normally passes. Traffic through the strait has been severely disrupted during the conflict, and Iranian attacks on tankers have increased in recent weeks. US crude traded near $97 a barrel on Thursday, close to the $100 mark. Supply concerns kept prices elevated despite moves by IEA members to speed up releases of emergency oil stocks.

The remarks are unlikely to shift oil prices much on their own, since they largely restate positions Trump has taken before. But they suggest a strike on Iran’s remaining nuclear infrastructure remains a live option once the pre-election pause ends, keeping a geopolitical risk premium in crude.

The next markers will be any sign of progress in contacts with Tehran before the midterms, further attacks on shipping in Hormuz, and whether Washington’s stated pause holds. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: India curbs gold ETF buying before Diwali, removing a seasonal prop for gold demand
item.description:
The curbs trim a traditional seasonal support for gold just as Indian festive demand would normally pick up. That adds to pressure on prices, which have already been weighed down by rising expectations of further US rate hikes rather than lifted by geopolitical risk. Physical buying through jewellers is unaffected, so the hit to overall Indian demand may be limited, but the ETF channel has been a growing source of fresh investment flows. Oil remains the root cause: higher crude prices have swollen India’s import bill and weakened the rupee, so a sustained move in oil will shape how long the restrictions stay in place.

--- India wants its citizens to celebrate Diwali with a little less gold, and the bullion market loses one of its more dependable autumn buyers.

Summary:

  • Kotak Mahindra, UTI and HDFC mutual funds are among those suspending bulk subscriptions to gold ETFs
  • The halt reportedly followed discussions with market regulator SEBI, and redemptions are unaffected
  • The move comes ahead of Dussehra and Diwali, the peak season for gold buying in India
  • The rupee has been pressured by higher oil prices and foreign equity selling, and gold and silver import duties were raised earlier this year
  • Gold imports fell to $1.8 billion in September from $2.3 billion in August
  • A bullion dealer called the move a precaution against an October import surge

Gold faces the loss of one of its most reliable seasonal supports after several large Indian mutual funds suspended bulk subscriptions to gold exchange-traded funds, just as the country enters its peak buying season for the metal.

Fund houses including Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund, UTI Mutual Fund and HDFC Mutual Fund issued public notices late on Thursday halting bulk purchases of their gold ETFs, Reuters reported. The notices gave no reason, and redemptions remain unaffected. A mutual fund executive and two bullion industry officials told Reuters the move followed discussions with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the market regulator. SEBI did not respond to a request for comment outside business hours.

The timing matters for gold. India is the world’s second-largest consumer of the metal and relies on imports for most of its supply. Demand typically rises around Dussehra in October and Diwali in early November, when buying gold is considered auspicious. Inflows into gold and silver ETFs surged during last year’s festive season as investors sought alternatives to lacklustre equity returns.

The underlying concern is the rupee. The currency has been under pressure this year from higher oil prices, which have swollen the import bill, and from heavy foreign selling of Indian shares. Strong gold demand has added to the strain, prompting the government to raise import duties on gold and silver earlier this year. Several fund houses also capped large gold ETF investments in June as authorities sought to curb imports.

The move appears pre-emptive rather than a response to a current surge. Gold imports fell to $1.8 billion in September from $2.3 billion in August. A bullion dealer at a private bank told Reuters that imports had not added to the trade deficit in recent months, and described the halt as a precaution against a jump in imports during October.

For the gold market, the curbs remove a source of incremental demand at a time when prices have already been under pressure from rising expectations of further US interest rate increases. Retail investors can still buy physical gold, so festive demand will not disappear. However, limiting large ETF purchases narrows one channel that has added fresh buying in past seasons.

The key questions now are whether other fund houses follow, how long the suspensions last, and whether India’s October import figures show festive demand shifting into physical gold instead. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nike’s problem is demand, not tariffs: what Moody’s warning really signals
item.description:
Reading the outlook change as a demand story rather than a tariff story is a more negative signal for Nike shares, because demand problems tend to last longer and cannot be fixed by a shift in trade policy. Credit investors are likely to stay calm while the A2 rating holds, but a sustained run of falling earnings would put the rating itself in play. China-exposed consumer brands may face closer scrutiny, given the scale of Nike’s slump there. The 16–17 November investor day is the next catalyst for both the shares and the debt.

---

A year ago Moody’s worried about what tariffs would cost Nike, but now it is worried about whether shoppers, especially in China, will come back.

Summary:

  • Moody’s cited a longer turnaround and Nike’s strategic actions, not tariffs, in changing its outlook to negative
  • In 2025, Moody’s cut Nike to A2 on tariff cost pressure, with a stable outlook
  • Nike’s revenue fell about 4% last quarter, with Greater China down 26% in constant currency and Converse down 28%
  • Gross margin rose slightly, with no tariff hit quantified
  • The Pace restructuring carries about $1 billion of charges, with most savings arriving in fiscal 2029 and 2030
  • New duties on China and Vietnam goods are a future risk, and investor day on 16–17 November is the next marker

When Moody’s changed its outlook on Nike to negative this week, the obvious suspect was tariffs. A closer look at the agency’s reasoning and at Nike’s own latest results points somewhere else. The pressure on earnings is coming mainly from weak demand and the cost of the company’s turnaround, with tariffs a risk ahead rather than the main driver so far.

That distinction marks a shift from a year ago. When Moody’s cut Nike’s rating to A2 from A1 in 2025, it cited cost pressure from higher tariffs and moved the outlook to stable. This time, in its outlook change on Nike, the agency pointed instead to a turnaround taking longer than expected, falling revenue and earnings into fiscal 2028, and the drag from Nike’s own strategic actions.

Nike’s first-quarter figures support that reading. Revenue fell about 4% and missed forecasts, with sales in Greater China down 26% on a currency-neutral basis and the Converse brand down 28%. Nike’s direct-to-consumer business, including digital, also shrank. Yet the gross margin rose slightly, helped by lower logistics costs and currency moves, and the company did not quantify any tariff hit in the quarter. A tariff-driven squeeze would usually show up in margins first. Here the damage is in sales.

Part of the weakness is deliberate. Nike has been cutting back on discount-led online and off-price sales to rebuild the brand’s pricing power, which shrinks revenue in the short term by design. It has also launched a restructuring programme called Pace. Pace carries about $1 billion of charges and is expected to deliver around $2.5 billion of savings, with most of the benefit not arriving until fiscal 2029 and 2030. That timetable lines up closely with Moody’s expectation of pressure into fiscal 2028.

Tariffs have not disappeared from the picture. Nike benefited from a refund of nearly $1 billion after earlier tariffs were struck down, but new duties of 12.5% on goods from China and Vietnam took effect in late July and barely touched the latest quarter. Nike’s guidance cites higher input costs, so tariffs could add pressure from here.

The split matters for how investors read the story. Tariff costs can ease with a policy change, but demand problems, particularly in China, take longer to fix and depend on Nike winning back consumers. The partial offset is that some of the revenue decline is a choice, making this partly a managed reset rather than pure weakness.

Nike’s investor day on 16 and 17 November is the next marker. It will show whether management can set out a credible path back to growth, especially in China. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Two AI signals, one week: TSMC’s boom and Dell’s doubts show where demand really is
item.description:
The split favours companies supplying the largest cloud and AI spenders, such as chipmakers and advanced manufacturing, over hardware makers relying on broad corporate demand. That divergence is likely to persist in stock performance until enterprise orders show clearer growth. Memory prices are the swing factor: a levelling off would pressure hardware revenue, while continued strength would delay the reckoning. Upcoming results from the biggest cloud providers are the next major catalyst, since any sign of slowing AI budgets would undermine the bullish half of the picture.

The AI boom has not cracked. It has just revealed a split: the hyperscalers are spending as hard as ever, while corporate IT departments are still deciding.

Summary:

  • TSMC beat forecasts and raised its outlook, saying AI demand is extremely robust and outrunning supply
  • Barclays downgraded Dell, HPE and NetApp, arguing enterprise AI spending has not yet inflected
  • Barclays says higher memory prices, not demand, are flattering hardware revenue
  • The two views reflect different customer bases: hyperscalers versus ordinary businesses
  • The divergence points to concentrated rather than broad AI demand
  • Hyperscaler results, memory prices and enterprise orders are the markers to watch

Two of this week’s biggest technology stories appear to send opposite messages about artificial intelligence. Taken together, they suggest the AI boom is real but narrower than some valuations assume. Demand is concentrated among the largest cloud and AI companies rather than spreading evenly through corporate IT budgets.

The bullish signal came from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world’s largest contract chipmaker. Its third-quarter profit rose nearly 70%, it raised its full-year growth outlook, and Chief Executive C.C. Wei said AI demand remained extremely robust with no sign of a slowdown. High-performance computing, the segment that includes AI accelerators, now makes up more than two-thirds of TSMC’s revenue, and the company says supply still falls well short of demand.

The cautious signal came a day earlier from Barclays. In its downgrade of Dell, the bank argued that enterprise AI spending has yet to show a meaningful inflection. It said strong revenue at hardware makers owes much to higher memory chip prices being passed on to customers. Barclays applied the same reasoning to Hewlett Packard Enterprise and NetApp, and the selloff spread across AI hardware stocks.

These views are less contradictory than they look. TSMC’s customers are dominated by the chip designers supplying the largest cloud providers and AI developers, whose spending remains heavy. Dell and its peers depend more on ordinary businesses building their own AI capacity, which is where Barclays sees the gap between expectation and reality.

The distinction matters for investors. If AI demand is concentrated at the top, the companies supplying the biggest spenders are on firmer ground than those relying on broad corporate adoption. It also means part of the recent revenue growth in enterprise hardware reflects pricing rather than volume, which could reverse if memory prices level off.

There are reasons for caution on both sides. Concentrated demand depends on a small number of very large buyers continuing to spend, while enterprise adoption could still accelerate as businesses move from experiments to deployment. Neither trend is settled.

Several markers will help resolve the debate:

  • Hyperscaler spending plans: upcoming quarterly results from the largest cloud providers will show whether their AI budgets are still rising.
  • Memory prices: a levelling off would test how much hardware revenue growth is genuine demand.
  • Enterprise orders: hardware makers’ own results will show whether AI server sales are broadening beyond a handful of large customers.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: Dell shares slide 17% in two days as Barclays questions enterprise AI demand
item.description:
The follow-through selling puts AI hardware tied to enterprise demand under sustained pressure, with servers, storage and networking stocks most exposed. The call does not dispute spending by the largest cloud and AI companies, leaving chipmakers and hyperscaler suppliers on firmer ground. Memory prices are the key sensitivity: any sign they are levelling off would strengthen the bearish case for hardware revenue. With Dell still up sharply this year, positioning remains crowded, which raises the risk of further profit-taking until the company’s own results give investors fresh evidence.

---

Updating this, all intertwined with the tech sell off of course. 

---

Barclays asked whether Dell’s customers are buying more or just paying more for memory, and two days and 17% later, the market is still voting with its feet.

Summary:

  • Dell shares fell about 11% on Wednesday and about 7% on Thursday, a two-day drop of roughly 17%
  • The stock closed Thursday near $473, nearly 20% below its mid-September record
  • Barclays cut Dell to equal weight from overweight and its target to $574 from $603
  • HPE and NetApp were also downgraded to equal weight
  • Barclays argues higher memory prices, not enterprise AI demand, are lifting hardware revenue
  • Dell has still nearly quadrupled this year, despite the selloff

Shares of Dell Technologies extended their slide on Thursday, falling about 7% after an 11% drop on Wednesday. Investors were digesting a Barclays downgrade arguing that the company’s booming revenue owes more to rising memory chip prices than to a genuine pickup in business spending on artificial intelligence.

The two-day decline of roughly 17% took the stock to around $473 at Thursday’s close. That leaves Dell nearly 20% below its record close in mid-September, close to the threshold many investors use to define a bear market. Thursday’s losses came early, with the shares opening sharply lower and briefly trading down nearly 11% before recovering some ground.

Barclays analyst Tim Long cut Dell to equal weight from overweight and lowered his price target to $574 from $603. He also downgraded Hewlett Packard Enterprise and NetApp to equal weight, applying a similar argument across enterprise hardware.

The core of the Barclays case is that enterprise AI spending has yet to show a meaningful inflection. Instead, Long argued, much of the recent strength in hardware makers’ results reflects higher memory costs being passed through to customers. That lifts reported revenue without a matching rise in underlying demand. If memory prices normalise or fall, that support could fade and leave revenue exposed.

The selloff follows an extraordinary run. Even after two days of heavy losses, Dell shares have nearly quadrupled this year, leaving little room for disappointment. The timing also creates a sharp contrast with the company’s own message. A day before the downgrade, Chief Executive Michael Dell said enterprise AI demand was only just beginning and that demand for AI computing still exceeded supply.

The pressure spread across AI hardware, with server maker Super Micro Computer and networking group Arista Networks among the stocks that weakened, while the broader technology sector posted more modest losses. That pattern suggests investors treated the call as a warning about one corner of the AI trade, hardware tied to enterprise demand, rather than a verdict on AI spending as a whole. 

The follow-through selling on Thursday matters. A one-day drop on a downgrade can reflect a quick repricing, but a second day of heavy losses suggests investors are reassessing how much of Dell’s growth is durable. The next test will be Dell’s own results and guidance. They should show whether AI server orders are broadening across enterprise customers, and how much of its revenue growth comes from pricing rather than volume. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: TSMC profit jumps nearly 70% on AI demand, but margin outlook weighs on shares
item.description:
The results (released Thursday afternoon, Taiwan time) reinforce the AI investment theme for Asian chip and hardware stocks, with TSMC’s view that demand is outrunning capacity supportive for suppliers across the semiconductor supply chain. The share reaction shows how high expectations are, though: a beat alone is no longer enough, and investors are now trading margins and cash flow. Taiwan’s equity benchmark, where TSMC carries a heavy weighting, is likely to take its lead from how the stock trades in Taipei. Higher planned capital spending is a positive read-through for equipment makers.

---

Background:

  • TSMC set for sixth straight record profit as AI demand lifts Q3 earnings

---

TSMC delivered the AI boom in numbers and told investors it is not slowing, but with the beat priced in, the market chose to fret about margins and the bill for all those new fabs.

Summary:

  • Q3 net profit rose nearly 70% to about NT$763 billion, slightly above LSEG consensus
  • Revenue of about $47 billion beat the top of TSMC’s own guidance range
  • The gross margin was about 66%, down from Q2 on the early 2nm ramp
  • AI-heavy high-performance computing made up 68% of revenue, and 2nm reached 8% of wafer revenue
  • Q4 guidance is about $52 billion to $54 billion in revenue, with 2026 growth now seen at around 44%
  • 2026 capex was reaffirmed at $60 billion to $64 billion, and US-listed shares slipped after the results

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. reported a jump of nearly 70% in third-quarter net profit on Thursday and raised its full-year growth outlook, as demand for chips used in artificial intelligence showed no sign of easing. The results still failed to lift its shares, with investors focusing on softer margin guidance and a heavy spending programme.

Net profit rose to about NT$763 billion, slightly ahead of analyst estimates compiled by LSEG. Revenue reached about $47 billion, above the top of the company’s own guidance range. The gross margin of about 66% was well up on a year earlier but down from the second quarter. TSMC attributed the sequential dip mainly to the early ramp-up of its 2-nanometre production.

The shift towards AI is clear in the revenue mix. High-performance computing, the segment that includes AI accelerators, accounted for 68% of revenue, up from 57% a year earlier. The newest 2-nanometre technology made up 8% of wafer revenue, up from 3% in the previous quarter.

Chief Executive C.C. Wei said AI demand remained extremely robust and suggested it would probably outpace the company’s earlier long-term growth forecast. He said supply still falls well short of demand, with TSMC building close to 20 new fabs, most of them in Taiwan.

For the fourth quarter, TSMC guided revenue of about $52 billion to $54 billion and a gross margin of 65% to 67%, a midpoint slightly below the third quarter. It now expects full-year revenue growth of around 44% in US dollar terms, up from slightly above 40% in July. The company reaffirmed 2026 capital spending of $60 billion to $64 billion. It said investment over the next three years would be significantly higher than in the previous three.

Those last two points explain the muted market reaction. Margin guidance implies further dilution from the 2-nanometre ramp, while management said overseas factories, including in Arizona and Japan, will weigh more heavily on margins over time. Heavier capital spending also points to lower free cash flow in the near term. With strong growth already expected, the profit beat was not large enough to offset those concerns.

The longer-term message remains firmly positive for the AI supply chain. TSMC’s view that demand is running ahead of capacity, and its willingness to keep spending to meet it, suggests the investment cycle has further to run. The next tests are whether margins stabilise as 2-nanometre production matures, and whether customers’ AI spending plans hold up through next year.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Moody’s cuts Nike outlook to negative, sees earnings falling into fiscal 2028
item.description:
The outlook change is a modest negative for Nike’s bonds and adds to pressure on the shares, though the affirmed A2 rating limits any immediate impact on borrowing costs. The extended timeline for falling revenue and earnings is the more market-relevant signal, because it challenges expectations of a near-term recovery. A negative outlook raises the risk of a future downgrade, which would matter more for credit investors if earnings fail to stabilise. Broader consumer discretionary names may also face scrutiny over how long restructuring costs weigh on profits.

-

Moody’s has not downgraded Nike, but by pushing its recovery out to fiscal 2028 it has put a timer on how long the turnaround can drag before the rating follows.

Summary:

  • Moody’s changed Nike’s outlook to negative and affirmed its A2 rating
  • The agency said the turnaround is taking longer than it previously expected
  • It expects revenue and earnings to fall through the fiscal year ending May 2027 and into fiscal 2028
  • Nike’s strategic actions are expected to pressure earnings over that period
  • That pressure is expected to constrain Nike’s credit metrics

Moody’s Ratings has revised its outlook on Nike to negative while affirming the sportswear group’s A2 credit rating, citing a turnaround that is taking longer than the agency had previously expected.

In a statement released on Thursday, Moody’s said it expects Nike’s revenue and earnings to decline through the fiscal year ending in May 2027 and into fiscal 2028. It added that the company’s strategic actions are likely to weigh on earnings over that period, which would constrain its credit metrics.

The decision stops short of a downgrade. An A2 rating sits in the upper-medium tier of investment grade, and affirming it signals that Moody’s still views Nike’s credit profile as solid. A negative outlook, however, indicates the agency sees a greater chance that the rating could be lowered if performance does not improve as expected. Outlook changes of this kind are typically reviewed over the following 12 to 18 months.

The key message for investors lies in the timeline. By extending its expectation of falling sales and profits well into fiscal 2028, Moody’s is effectively signalling that the recovery in Nike’s business is further away than it had assumed. The emphasis on strategic actions suggests the costs of repositioning the business, rather than any single external shock, are a central part of the pressure on earnings.

For bondholders, the move is more of a warning than an immediate change in risk, since the rating itself is unchanged. For equity investors, it adds an independent voice to concerns about how long the turnaround will take. It also puts more weight on upcoming quarterly results as evidence of whether the business is stabilising.

The next test will be Nike’s own guidance and trading updates. They will show whether revenue declines are narrowing or, as Moody’s expects, continuing beyond the current financial year. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: New Zealand card spending falls for second month as food prices hold flat in September
item.description:
The data adds to a mixed picture for the New Zealand dollar, with weak household spending offsetting the stronger manufacturing survey released earlier in the day. A second monthly fall in card spending points to soft domestic demand, which tends to argue against tighter policy, while flat food prices remove one source of upward pressure on inflation for the month. Fuel costs, which manufacturers flagged as a key concern, remain the bigger swing factor for household budgets, leaving oil prices important for the consumer outlook.

---

Yesterday:

  • RBNZ’s Conway says October rate decision completely open, OCR more likely to rise

---

New Zealand’s factories are finding their stride, but its shoppers are still keeping their cards in their wallets, and flat food prices are only a modest consolation.

Summary:

  • Seasonally adjusted electronic card retail spending fell 0.4% in September, after a 0.9% drop in August
  • Actual card spending rose 0.9% from a year earlier, up from 0.2% in August
  • Card data covers about 68% of core retail sales
  • Food prices were unchanged on the month, after a 0.3% rise in August, and up 2.4% on the year
  • Food accounts for nearly 19% of the consumers price index
  • The weak consumer data contrasts with a strong manufacturing PMI released the same day

New Zealand electronic card retail spending fell for a second straight month in September, while food prices held steady, according to data from Statistics New Zealand on Friday. The figures point to cautious households even as other parts of the economy show more life.

Seasonally adjusted retail spending on electronic cards slipped 0.4% from August, following a 0.9% decline the previous month. In unadjusted terms, actual spending was 0.9% higher than in September last year, a firmer annual pace than the 0.2% recorded in August. Electronic card transactions cover roughly 68% of core retail sales and are the main monthly gauge of retail activity in New Zealand.

The figures suggest consumers remain under pressure. Back-to-back monthly declines in spending, after seasonal adjustment, point to households trimming discretionary purchases, while the annual rise in actual spending is modest. Because the card data measures the value of transactions rather than volumes, part of that rise reflects higher prices.

Separately, Statistics New Zealand’s food price index was unchanged in September from August, after a 0.3% rise the month before. Food prices were 2.4% higher than a year earlier. Food carries a weight of nearly 19% in the consumers price index, so a flat monthly reading removes one source of upward pressure on headline inflation for the month.

The softer consumer data contrasts with a stronger picture from manufacturers. The BNZ-BusinessNZ manufacturing index released earlier on Friday showed the sector expanding at a much stronger rate in September. However, many firms cited fuel prices, cost of living pressures and uncertainty ahead of the election as concerns.

Taken together, the releases describe an economy where production and orders are picking up but household spending is lagging, held back by living costs. A pause in food price growth offers some relief. On its own, however, it is unlikely to change the broader picture for household budgets while fuel costs stay elevated.

The next indications of consumer strength will come from upcoming retail and inflation data. They will show whether September’s weakness in card spending persists into the final quarter, when pre-Christmas demand typically provides a seasonal lift.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
