Hammack is less worried about where inflation is today than about Americans starting to expect it, and that distinction could lower her bar for backing another hike.

Summary:

  • Hammack said a worsening of inflation expectations would likely require more aggressive Fed action
  • Warned that an inflationary mindset would make monetary policy’s job much harder
  • Businesses are seeing significant input cost pressures, and lower-income Americans are struggling with inflation
  • Said it is hard to know where the neutral rate sits
  • Said financial conditions do not currently appear restrictive
  • Was speaking at a Goldman Sachs event in New York

Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack warned on Thursday that a deterioration in the public’s inflation expectations would likely require a more forceful response from the central bank. Her remarks add to signs that policymakers are prepared to keep tightening.

Speaking at an event hosted by Goldman Sachs in New York, Hammack said her main concern was the emergence of an inflationary mindset, in which households and businesses come to expect persistent price pressures. If that took hold, she said, it would become much harder for monetary policy to do its job, and the Fed might need to move further than it otherwise would.

Hammack said businesses were reporting substantial pressure from input costs, and that she was hearing more from lower-income Americans who are struggling with inflation. She stressed the value of anecdotal reports from businesses and communities as a guide to the economy, alongside official data.

On the policy stance, Hammack said it is difficult to pin down where the neutral interest rate lies, the level that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. She added that financial conditions do not currently appear restrictive. That view implies current settings may not be doing enough to bring inflation down.

Her comments come with the Fed already on a hiking path. The central bank raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4.00% in September, its first increase in this cycle, and policymakers next meet on 27 and 28 October. Hammack votes on policy this year.

Taken together, the remarks point to a preference for further tightening rather than any pause. Her emphasis on expectations, rather than the current inflation rate alone, matters. It suggests her threshold for supporting another hike could be lower if surveys or business reports show price pressures becoming entrenched. At the same time, she did not commit to the timing of any move.

The comments are likely to reinforce market attention on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who speaks later in the Asian session, and on upcoming measures of inflation expectations. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: New Zealand manufacturing PMI jumps to 56.5, 15th straight month of expansion
item.description:
The stronger reading is mildly supportive for the New Zealand dollar, adding to evidence that the goods side of the economy is gathering pace into year-end. Firm new orders and production point to near-term resilience, while the return to growth in employment is the detail policymakers are likely to watch most closely. Fuel prices remain the main cost pressure cited by firms, so any further rise in oil prices would squeeze margins and could dent sentiment that is already more negative than the headline suggests. Election uncertainty adds a domestic risk premium to investment decisions.

Newswire cut: New Zealand’s BNZ-BusinessNZ manufacturing PMI jumped to 56.5 in September from 53.3, its 15th straight month of expansion, led by finished stocks and deliveries, as employment also returned to growth despite fuel costs and election uncertainty.

One-line wrap: New Zealand’s factories posted their strongest month since 2021 outside of June, but the firms behind the numbers sound far less cheerful than the index.

Summary:

  • The seasonally adjusted PMI rose 3.2 points to 56.5 in September, above the long-run average of 52.5
  • The sector has now expanded for 15 consecutive months
  • Finished stocks (59.0) and deliveries (58.8) led, with production and new orders both at 57.0
  • Employment was the weakest sub-index at 51.8, but returned to expansion from 50.0
  • Setting aside June’s 60.1, it was the highest reading since 2021
  • 53% of respondent comments were negative, citing fuel prices and election uncertainty

New Zealand’s manufacturing sector expanded at a markedly faster pace in September, with the BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Manufacturing Index rising to 56.5 from 53.3 in August. The seasonally adjusted reading sits well above the survey’s long-run average of 52.5. It marks a 15th consecutive month above the 50 level that separates expansion from contraction.

The improvement was broad. Finished stocks led the sub-indices at 59.0, followed by deliveries at 58.8, while production and new orders both climbed strongly to 57.0. Employment was the softest component at 51.8, but it moved back into expansion after sitting at 50.0, the no-change mark, in August.

BusinessNZ Director of Advocacy Catherine Beard welcomed the result. She pointed to the return to growth in employment as a possible sign that manufacturers are becoming more willing to hire. She said strength across new orders, production and finished stocks suggested genuine momentum heading into the final quarter, although respondents were still weighing cost of living pressures.

BNZ Senior Economist Doug Steel said that, setting aside June’s unusually strong reading of 60.1, September’s figure was the highest since 2021. He described it as an impressive outcome given the range of domestic and international headwinds facing the sector.

The upbeat headline did not translate fully into business mood. Just over half of respondents’ comments were negative, with firms continuing to cite fuel prices and uncertainty ahead of the election. Others pointed to seasonal lifts in activity, orders placed ahead of Christmas and firmer demand as reasons for optimism.

That contrast is the key caveat for readers. Strong forward-looking components such as new orders suggest activity should hold up in the near term. However, elevated fuel costs and election uncertainty could weigh on investment and hiring decisions if they persist. Part of September’s lift may also reflect seasonal and pre-Christmas ordering rather than a lasting shift in demand.

The next test will be whether October’s survey confirms the momentum, particularly in employment, which remains the weakest part of the picture.  

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Warsh speaks in Bangkok after hot CPI: is a second Fed hike coming in October?
item.description:
This is the highest-impact appearance of the day. Short-dated Treasuries and the dollar are most exposed to any signal that October is live, after Wednesday’s inflation data lifted two-year yields sharply. Oil is the central variable: fuel costs tied to the Iran war are the main source of the latest inflation jump, so a sustained move in crude feeds directly into Fed hike expectations. A hawkish Warsh would likely add pressure on equities and gold, which slid after the CPI release as yields rose. A guarded performance, sticking to his dislike of forward guidance, would leave the hike debate resting on data.

---

Warsh is the big one today! But not the only one:

  • BOE, Bailey, Bangkok. What could possibly go wrong? Preview and 3 questions for the Governor
  • Preview: Nagel and Klingbeil in Bangkok: three themes as the ECB weighs a December hike
  • Macklem in Bangkok: oil, tariffs and job losses test the Bank of Canada’s hike case

---

Warsh has spent two months arguing inflation will not fix itself, and a hot September CPI hands him the evidence just as markets debate whether the Fed’s second hike comes in October or December.

Summary:

  • Warsh appears in a moderated conversation at the IMF meetings in Bangkok at 03:30 GMT (23:30 ET Thursday)
  • The Fed raised rates by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00% in September, its first hike since 2023, on a unanimous vote
  • September CPI beat forecasts, with headline and core inflation both rising on higher fuel costs
  • Hiring has slowed sharply, but unemployment remains low and within a narrow range
  • Most Fed officials projected at least one more hike this year; the next meeting is 27-28 October
  • Warsh has said inflation is the bigger concern and opposes giving forward guidance

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh appears in a moderated conversation at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday, days after US inflation data strengthened the case for further tightening. The session is scheduled for 03:30 GMT (23:30 US Eastern on Thursday), less than two weeks before the Federal Open Market Committee meets on 27 and 28 October.

The Fed is on a hiking path. In September it raised the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4.00%, its first increase since 2023, according to the Fed’s published statement. The vote was unanimous. The move reversed the last of three quarter-point cuts delivered in late 2025 and signalled a clear shift in priorities towards inflation.

That shift was driven by prices. Inflation has run above the Fed’s 2% goal for years, and higher fuel costs linked to the Iran war have pushed it further from target. September consumer price data released on Wednesday showed headline inflation rising again and beating forecasts, with core inflation also edging higher. The Fed said in September that inflation remains elevated and that its decision would support a timelier return to target.

The labour market, the other half of the Fed’s dual mandate, is less of a constraint for now. Hiring has slowed markedly in recent months and earlier figures have been revised lower. However, the unemployment rate has stayed within a narrow range and remains low by historical standards.

Warsh has made his priorities clear. In his Jackson Hole speech in August he said inflation was too high and would not return to target on its own, arguing that underlying price pressures had not meaningfully improved. He judged inflation a bigger concern than the jobs market. He also said current rates were not restricting activity given strong investment and consumer spending, and described short-term rates as the Fed’s main tool against inflation. He has also said he opposes giving forward guidance on future meetings.

Other officials have leaned the same way. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack is a voter this year and dissented in favour of a hike in July. She said this week she believes rates need to rise further to restrain demand, while keeping an open mind on the timing.

Markets had leaned towards a hold in October after a weak September jobs report. Wednesday’s inflation data pushed Treasury yields higher as traders added to bets on further tightening. In September, most Fed officials projected at least one more increase by year-end.

Several things are worth watching:

  • October: whether Warsh signals that an October move is live, or keeps to his line against previewing decisions.
  • Energy: how he characterises the fuel-driven rise in inflation, and whether he sees signs of it spreading into wider prices and expectations.
  • Jobs: whether the slowdown in hiring features in his assessment at all.
  • AI investment: given the IMF setting, whether he returns to his argument that strong AI-related investment is one reason current rates are not holding back activity.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Macklem in Bangkok: oil, tariffs and job losses test the Bank of Canada’s hike case
item.description:
The Canadian dollar and short-dated Canada yields are most exposed if Macklem is drawn on policy. With October hike odds already slashed after the jobs data, any hawkish signal would carry more surprise value than a cautious one. Oil cuts both ways for Canada: higher crude supports the terms of trade and the currency, but it is also the main source of above-target inflation, so a sustained move in prices would shift both the inflation debate and the loonie. Tariff headlines remain a second source of volatility.

---

Earlier:

  • Economic and event calendar in Asia Friday, October 16, 2026 - Federal Reserve Chair Warsh speaking
  • BOE, Bailey, Bangkok. What could possibly go wrong? Preview and 3 questions for the Governor
  • Preview: Nagel and Klingbeil in Bangkok: three themes as the ECB weighs a December hike

---

Macklem has argued the Bank can look through an oil shock only until it spreads, and two months of job losses have made markets doubt the spreading starts soon enough to justify an October hike.

Summary:

  • Macklem speaks on an IMF panel on AI and the global economy in Bangkok at 04:15 GMT (00:15 ET)
  • The policy rate is 2.25%, unchanged since a cut in October 2025
  • Headline inflation is above target on gasoline prices, while core measures sit near 2%
  • New US tariffs and back-to-back monthly job losses have weakened the growth outlook
  • Markets have cut the odds of an October hike, but still lean towards a move by December
  • The next decision is 28 October, with September inflation data due on Monday

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem joins a panel on artificial intelligence and the global economy at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday. It comes less than two weeks before the central bank’s 28 October rate decision. The session is scheduled for 04:15 GMT (00:15 US Eastern), according to the Bank’s media advisory. The topic is AI rather than monetary policy, so any comments on rates would most likely come in response to questions.

The policy rate stands at 2.25%, where it has been since a quarter-point cut in October last year, according to the Bank of Canada. Governing Council has held at every decision since. The most recent hold was on 2 September, when it said it was prepared to adjust policy as needed.

Headline inflation is running above the 2% target, pushed up by higher gasoline prices linked to the Middle East conflict and damaged refining capacity. Core measures, however, have stayed close to target, and the Bank has said it sees little sign so far of energy costs spreading into wider prices. In a speech last month, Macklem said the Bank can look through the direct effect of higher oil, but only while those pressures stay contained. He added that it does not want to be too slow to respond if they broaden.

The growth picture complicates the decision. The economy rebounded strongly in the second quarter. However, new US tariffs following the breakdown of Canada-US trade talks have clouded the outlook, and Macklem has warned growth could slow sharply late this year if they persist.

The labour market has also turned. Canada shed jobs in both August and September, and the unemployment rate rose back to where it started the year. That points to continued slack in the economy.

The jobs data shifted expectations. Markets scaled back the odds of an October hike to well below even after the September report, while still leaning towards a move by December. Some economists now expect the Bank to hold this month, though others had been forecasting an increase.

Three questions matter if Macklem is drawn on policy:

  • Inflation risk: whether he still sees energy-driven inflation as the bigger risk, or gives more weight to the weaker jobs market.
  • Tariffs: how he judges the growth hit from US tariffs.
  • October: whether he leaves the door open to a move this month. September inflation data on Monday is the next marker.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Preview: Nagel and Klingbeil in Bangkok: three themes as the ECB weighs a December hike
item.description:
The euro and short-dated Bunds are most sensitive to any steer from Nagel on December. A clear endorsement of a further hike would firm rate support for the single currency. Any nod to French fiscal strain as a reason for caution would point the other way. Oil remains the key driver of the ECB debate: Nagel has called it one of the indicators the Governing Council must now watch, so a sustained easing in crude and gas prices would weaken the case for more tightening. Klingbeil’s comments on German spending matter for Bund supply and longer-dated yields.

---

It's a huge session for central bank speakers today:

  • Economic and event calendar in Asia Friday, October 16, 2026 - Federal Reserve Chair Warsh speaking
  • BOE, Bailey, Bangkok. What could possibly go wrong? Preview and 3 questions for the Governor

---

Nagel is in Bangkok as one of the ECB’s firmer voices on tightening, but questions on French debt could test how far he is willing to push.

Summary:

  • Nagel and Klingbeil hold a joint press conference in Bangkok at 02:30 GMT (22:30 ET Thursday)
  • The ECB raised its deposit rate in June and September, taking it to 2.50%
  • Euro area inflation is well above target and rose again in September on energy costs
  • Nagel says rates are around neutral but has not ruled out mildly restrictive settings
  • Markets and most economists expect a hold on 29 October and a hike in December
  • French bond spreads and Germany’s improving growth outlook are likely press conference themes

Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel holds a joint press conference with German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil in Bangkok on Friday, on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings. It comes less than two weeks before the European Central Bank’s 29 October policy decision. The briefing is scheduled for 02:30 GMT (22:30 US Eastern on Thursday).

The ECB has been on a tightening path since the Iran war pushed energy costs higher. It raised its deposit rate by a quarter point in June and again in September, taking it to 2.50%, according to the ECB’s published key rates. Before that, the rate had been held at 2% for a year.

Euro area inflation is running well above the 2% target and climbed further in September, driven mainly by energy. The ECB’s own September projections show inflation staying above target well into next year, with underlying price pressures still building into early 2027. The labour market has held steady, and wage growth has so far shown little response to the energy shock.

Nagel is one of the Governing Council’s more hawkish voices. He said in late September that rates sit around neutral, but that a move into mildly restrictive territory could not be ruled out if price pressures persist. He has since argued that high uncertainty calls for flexibility rather than inaction, flagging low European gas storage as a particular vulnerability.

Germany offers a brighter backdrop than it has for some time. Nagel has described a gradual recovery supported by foreign orders and public spending on infrastructure and defence. Berlin this month sharply raised its growth forecast for this year.

Markets and most economists expect the ECB to hold in October before a further hike in December. Citigroup has argued that French fiscal strain could make December the last move. French bond spreads over Germany widened earlier this month to their highest in well over a decade.

Three themes are likely to dominate the briefing:

  • December: whether Nagel backs a further hike or leans towards waiting.
  • France: how he answers questions on French debt, having said the ECB’s bond-market backstop is not designed to fix individual countries’ fiscal problems.
  • German fiscal policy: what Klingbeil signals on German spending and borrowing, which feeds directly into Bund supply.++
This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOE, Bailey, Bangkok. What could possibly go wrong? Preview and 3 questions for the Governor
item.description:
Sterling and short-dated gilts are most exposed to Bailey’s remarks, because front-end pricing already assumes a November hike is close to a done deal. If he endorses that view, rate support for the pound stays in place. Any hint of patience, or emphasis on the softer jobs market, could pull hike odds lower and weigh on the currency. Oil remains the swing factor: the Bank’s case for tightening rests on oil and gas prices staying well above pre-war levels, so any easing in Brent would weaken the hawkish argument more than anything Bailey says.

---

Bailey has spent a month telling markets that high energy prices are making a hold harder to justify, and Bangkok is his chance to confirm or cool a November hike they have almost fully priced.

Summary:

  • Bailey appears in conversation at the IIF annual membership meeting in Bangkok at 02:00 GMT (22:00 ET Thursday)
  • Bank Rate is 3.75%, unchanged since a 5-4 vote to cut last December
  • The MPC held 6-3 in September, with three members voting to hike to 4% and Bailey voting to hold
  • Inflation is well above the 2% target and expected to rise further as Iran war energy costs feed through
  • The labour market has softened, which is the main argument for waiting
  • Markets and most economists expect a hike at the 5 November meeting, a week after the 28 October Budget

Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey takes the stage at the Institute of International Finance’s annual membership meeting in Bangkok, held alongside the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, on Friday, with financial markets increasingly convinced that the Bank’s next move will be a rate rise. Bailey is due to appear in conversation with IIF President and Chief Executive Tim Adams at 02:00 GMT (22:00 US Eastern on Thursday), less than three weeks before the Monetary Policy Committee’s 5 November decision.

Bank Rate stands at 3.75%, where it has been since a narrow 5-4 vote delivered a quarter-point cut last December. At its most recent meeting in September, the MPC held the rate by a 6-3 majority, according to the Bank’s published minutes. Bailey was among the six voting to hold, and the other three preferred an immediate increase to 4%.

Inflation is the central problem. Consumer price inflation is running well above the 2% target, as it has for almost all of the past five years. The Bank expects it to climb further into early next year as higher oil, gas and electricity costs linked to the Iran war work through to household bills. The Bank has said those costs have so far had only a limited effect on wider wage and price setting. It has also said that the longer energy prices stay high, the more likely it becomes that Bank Rate will need to rise.

The jobs market offers a partial counterweight. Unemployment has drifted higher and private-sector pay growth has eased, and the slack that implies is a key reason the majority preferred to wait in September.

Bailey’s tone has hardened since that vote. He warned in late September that persistently high energy prices would make it harder to keep rates on hold, adding that the Bank could not wait for complete evidence on inflation expectations. He has since argued that looking through an energy shock only works while expectations stay anchored. Markets have taken the hint: traders price a high probability of a November hike, and a Reuters poll this week found a large majority of economists expect Bank Rate to rise to 4%.

Three questions will shape the reaction:

  • November pricing: whether Bailey endorses it or pushes back, having previously told lawmakers the Bank has no unconditional plan for rates.
  • The Budget: how much weight he gives the 28 October Budget, which lands a week before the decision.
  • The labour market: whether he dwells on its softness, which would suggest the majority is not yet ready to move. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Dow leads US stock rebound. Indices snatch victory from the jaws of defeat.
item.description:
Snatching victory from the jaws of defeat.

The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite closed higher after buyers turned a difficult session for technology shares into a recovery. The Nasdaq 100 could not quite complete the comeback, but its modest decline looked considerably better than the losses earlier in the day.

The Dow industrial average led the large-cap indices higher, with Nike topping its percentage gainers. Small caps also participated, with the Russell 2000 rising 1.38%. The recovery extended beyond the biggest technology names, although pockets of heavy selling remained among semiconductor and AI infrastructure shares.

The closing numbers

  • Dow Industrial Average: +557.06 points, or +1.08%, at 52,183.23.

  • S&P 500: +25.15 points, or +0.33%, at 7,744.09.

  • Nasdaq Composite: +20.16 points, or +0.08%, at 26,713.03.

  • Russell 2000: +37.74 points, or +1.38%, at 2,767.28.

  • Nasdaq 100: −15.22 points, or −0.05%, at 29,935.59.

Those closing changes do not tell the whole story.

At the lows, the S&P was down 49.28 points. The Nasdaq Composite was down 384.02 points, while the Nasdaq 100 was down 542.40 points.

By the close, the S&P had recovered 74.43 points from its low, and the Nasdaq Composite had recovered 404.18 points. The Nasdaq 100 briefly traded up 34.81 points before slipping back below unchanged.

The Dow had a different day. It stayed positive throughout the session, with even its low showing a gain of around 60 points.

The sellers had their shot in the broader indices. They could not keep the downside momentum going.

Nike leads the Dow’s percentage gainers

Nike rose 5.27%, leading a strong group of Dow performers. The gain today was a welcome bounce in what has been a difficult year. Even after closing at $37.16, the shares remain down roughly 42% in 2026, underscoring how much ground buyers still need to recover. The low after earnings on October 1 reached $31.97. That was the lowest level going back to 2013.  Leading the Dow’s percentage gainers gives buyers something to build on, but one strong session does not reverse the broader trend. The next test is whether today’s buying attracts follow-through. The top 5 winners in the Dow today were: 

  • Nike: +5.27%.

  • Salesforce: +4.52%.

  • Home Depot: +4.33%.

  • Sherwin-Williams: +3.83%.

  • UnitedHealth: +2.83%.

That strength helped distinguish the Dow from the more technology-heavy Nasdaq indices.

The Magnificent 7 finish mixed

The biggest technology names did not move together:

  • Microsoft: +1.08%.

  • Alphabet: +0.45%.

  • Amazon: +0.27%.

  • Meta: −0.11%.

  • Apple: −0.28%.

  • Tesla: −1.29%.

  • Nvidia: −1.84%.

Nvidia deserves a closer look. The shares closed at $217.23 after falling to $212.85 earlier in the session. That low briefly took the price below both its 100-day moving average at $214.47 and the 38.2% retracement at $213.15. Buyers responded, pushing the price back above both technical levels.

The stock still finished lower, but the recovery gives traders a defined area to watch. Stay above that support area, and buyers have something to build on. Move back below it and stay below it, and the recovery becomes more vulnerable.

Big winners—and losses that did not disappear

Among the stronger individual performers:

  • Roblox: +7.57%.

  • Macy’s: +6.75%.

  • AppLovin: +6.52%.

  • Intuit: +6.36%.

  • Coinbase: +6.32%.

  • SoFi Technologies: +6.12%.

  • CoreWeave: +5.96%.

  • Lennar: +5.66%.

  • Strategy: +5.62%.

However, the index recovery did not erase the damage everywhere. Several chip, networking and AI infrastructure shares still finished sharply lower:

  • Dell Technologies: −6.92%.

  • Arista Networks: −5.05%.

  • Applied Materials: −3.72%.

  • Vertiv: −3.61%.

  • Cisco: −3.35%.

  • Lam Research: −3.30%.

  • Intel: −2.81%.

CoreWeave’s gain also shows why traders need to judge individual stocks on their own price action. Even within a related group, the results can differ considerably.

Trading lesson: a recovery needs follow-through

A sharp intraday recovery tells us that sellers could not maintain control through the close. That matters. It does not, by itself, confirm that the broader decline is over.

Nvidia provides a practical example. Its moving average and retracement gave traders a support area against which to define risk. Sellers briefly pushed below it, but could not sustain the break.

Now the buyers need to build on that defense.

The same principle applies to the broader market heading into Friday: today’s recovery gives buyers a starting point. Holding the recovery and reclaiming overhead resistance would give them more control. Renewed selling that erases the rebound would weaken their case.

Watch the levels, define the risk, and wait for the next shove.
